Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette: Tane, a 56-year-old detective of Māori descent, recalls the night he was dragged from the small, flickering kitchen of his childhood home. The caretaker had poured boiling water over his brother's arm, a reckless act that left a lingering, acrid scent of burnt plastic on the air. When Tane later walked past the same stove in a case involving a kitchen fire, the smell surged through him, jolting a flash of that childhood terror. The memory of the caretaker's snarled face and the boy's screams, coupled with the vivid, searing odor, immediately triggered a surge of rage and a physical reactivity that made his heart pound, his shoulders tighten, and his fingers clamp over his coffee mug. To keep the torrent of feeling from overtaking him, he began shunning the color of his brother's hoodie and the gray coats worn by his partner, avoiding any clothing that mirrored the battered, blue-tinted attire of the victim he had once witnessed. The instinct to detach himself from the recollection-drawing a mental wall between past and present-became a coping tactic he relied on whenever a similar scent or sight stirred the buried nightmare. The intrusive recall of that night does not stay locked in the past. As soon as Tane's mind turns back to the caretaker's violent grip, the body springs into hypervigilance: his eyes scan the room for a second flame, his muscles tense in readiness to flee or fight. Sleep becomes a battle; he wakes with the sense that the darkness is a blanket of threat, staying alert through the night, unable to find rest. In the quiet moments between raids, his mind replays the incident, magnifying the sense that the world operates on cruelty and betrayal. Each time the memory surfaces, it throws him into a loop of shattered beliefs-"no one is safe" becomes a mantra-and it cements the conviction that he is a bad coper, that the only way he survived was by becoming a monster himself. The memory also reignites the same triggers: the scent of burnt plastic, the sight of a stranger who bears a resemblance to the caretaker, and even a fleeting, misplaced laugh that he misinterprets as a positive emotion, which in reality feels more like a mocking echo of the past. Because Tane believes that the abuse was a result of "the kind of person I am," he interprets the memory as proof of his inherent flaw. This belief loop feeds back into the memory, each recall tightening his self-blame. The constant physical reactivity that follows each recollection-his jaw clenches, his chest tightens-reinforces the idea that the world is unforgiving. The threat he feels is not abstract; it is a visceral, embodied warning that the same caretaker could appear again, that any stranger might be a threat. This heightened perception of danger amplifies his conviction that he cannot trust others, solidifying his negative appraisal of himself as a "bad coper" who must remain on guard at all times. Tane's avoidance of people and similar clothing further isolates him from ordinary interactions. When he detaches from a memory, he does so by shutting the emotional channel, creating a cognitive break that is easy in the moment but keeps the memory alive in a half-remembered, detached state. This detachment allows the memory to persist, because the mind still recognizes the event's pattern even when it is emotionally numbed. His avoidance strategies-steering clear of anyone who resembles the caretaker, wearing uniforms that clash with his past trauma, and refusing to engage in social contact-create new opportunities for triggers. A co-worker's casual comment about "old times" triggers the memory again; the smell of burnt coffee in a break room sends him into hypervigilance, and he retreats to the solitude of his desk, reinforcing the cycle. By avoiding people, he denies the chance to test his fear and, in doing so, sustains the belief that he cannot cope; the cycle tightens as each avoidance strengthens the next trigger. In his current role, Tane often finds himself in scenes that mirror the elements of his childhood trauma: crime scenes with lingering burnt odors, victims with bruised faces that remind him of his brother, colleagues who, unknowingly, look like the caretaker in a different light. These environments serve as daily reminders that the past is not a closed chapter; they force him to confront the triggers and memories that have been the engine of his threat perception. He now finds that the very job that gave him purpose also serves as a constant source of fear, preventing him from sleeping and from forming new, healthy relationships. It was the cumulative toll of nights spent staring at a ceiling that seemed to whisper danger, of missing family gatherings because he could not bear the thought of being around others, and of a growing conviction that he was forever damaged that pushed Tane to seek therapy. He comes with a fear of the day when his memory of that kitchen fire will return with such intensity that he can no longer control his rage or his physical reactivity. He hopes, however, to learn a way to walk into a kitchen without that scent turning his world upside down, to believe that he can be both a detective and a person who is more than a victim, and to rebuild the fractured sense that people can be trusted.
